transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, Elysian), Rajiv Menon (Head of Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Security)

Summary (auto):
Quick intro, confirm success criteria for a 4-week POC focused on private networking and data residency. Main asks: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, regions (EU/UK), egress restrictions (no public egress), performance targets (p95 latency, throughput), and benchmark plan. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics:
- Private networking: VPC peering vs PrivateLink and implications
- Regions & data residency (EU, UK)
- Egress constraints and firewall rules
- Workload sizing and benchmark success criteria
- POC timeline and deliverables

Action items (in-call): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm laura from redwood, im the ae on this account, and daniel who is our se will run through the networking bits. hows everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya Patel: hey laura hi daniel doing good thanks, we were hoping to lock down the networking approach today and agree success criteria for the poc.
[00:12] Daniel Ortiz: great, i'll do a quick framing then we can dig into the VPC questions and benchmarks. just to confirm, this is a 4 week poc request from your side?
[00:20] Maya Patel: yeah ideally 4 weeks, maybe slightly flexible depending on scheduling and approvals. main constraints: all traffic must not egress to the public internet from our VPC, data residency for EU/UK, and we need measurable latency/throughput targets for our conversational assistant workload.
[00:33] Rajiv Menon: also we use AWS exclusively today, we'd prefer peering or PrivateLink — whichever gives us simpler security posture and less operational overhead. our infra team is small, so managed solutions are preferred.
[00:42] Daniel Ortiz: understood. quick high level: Redwood supports both VPC peering (or transit gateway) and AWS PrivateLink. Peering has slightly lower latency typically but requires route table adjustments and can be harder across accounts/regions; PrivateLink provides endpoint services and keeps traffic within the AZs and managed ENIs, it's easier for controlled egress policies but can add latency in some topologies.
[01:05] Sofia Alvarez: can you clarify the egress model? when you say "within AZs", do you mean traffic still leaves our VPC and hits your managed infra in another account, or is there an option for us to deploy private control plane inside our VPC?
[01:16] Daniel Ortiz: good question. for Hosted Redwood we run a managed control plane in our tenancy; networking options for private connectivity are: 1) VPC peering to a customer-dedicated subnet on our side (we use cross-account peering patterns), 2) PrivateLink endpoint service where the customer owns the endpoint and AWS handles the ENI, or 3) Private (on-prem/VPC) deployment — for larger customers we can deploy a Private control plane in their VPC or VPCs. the Private deployment eliminates cross-account egress because the inference runtime is inside your VPC. but that has more setup and typically moves to our Private product offering.
[01:52] Maya Patel: ok so we need to pick between PrivateLink and peering for the poc. our security team prefers PrivateLink historically because you avoid broad route table exposure. is there any limitation on model versions or throughput for PrivateLink vs peering?
[02:06] Daniel Ortiz: functionally no limitations on model family, but throughput is more about the underlying instance types and the capacity we provision. for the poc we can allocate dedicated capacity to match your target throughput. PrivateLink adds a bit of latency usually in the 5-15ms ballpark, peering can shave that off if in same AZ/region. for your workloads, what are you targeting?
[02:28] Rajiv Menon: peak is around 50 rps for prompt inference (average 200 tokens per request), we want p95 end-to-end latency under 150ms for the majority of calls. cost is a concern but first priority is meeting latency and residency.
[02:42] Daniel Ortiz: 50 RPS with ~200 tokens is a good anchor. we'll propose a config with two dedicated GPU nodes (A100 class or equivalent), continuous batching tuned for your request size, and KV cache warm-up. For benchmarking we recommend a synthetic load that mirrors your token distribution plus a set of real prompt samples. Our expectation is p95 under 150ms is achievable but we'll validate in the poc.
[03:04] Laura Kim: to add, success criteria we typically codify: 1) networking — no public egress for inference traffic; 2) data residency — all logs and model data stored in EU/UK region; 3) performance — p95 < 150ms, sustained 50 rps for 30 minutes; 4) cost estimate within agreed band. if those look right we can put them in the poc doc.
[03:26] Maya Patel: that aligns. one nuance — compliance will require audit logs and KMS integration. can you store logs in our S3 bucket and have KMS control?
[03:35] Daniel Ortiz: yes we support customer-managed KMS keys and shipping audit logs to your S3. for Hosted we can configure cross-account S3 writes and SSE-KMS using your key; for Private deployment this is straightforward since everything is in your account.
[03:49] Sofia Alvarez: also need SOC2 + ISO artifacts and details on key rotation, and retention policy for prompt traces. we will need the security pack before sign-off.
[03:57] Laura Kim: absolutely, i'll share the security pack link after this call. it's a short packet with SOC2/ISO attestations, our pen test summary, and KMS integration guide.
[04:06] Rajiv Menon: on egress controls — currently our VPC has strict egress rules, only whitelisted IP ranges for certain services. we can't allow dynamic outbound to internet. how do you handle outbound access from your runtime (for example model downloads, telemetry)?
[04:18] Daniel Ortiz: good detail. model artifacts are pre-provisioned for the poc; we can stage the model in-region and keep local caches. telemetry can be configured to use your endpoints (we can push telemetry to your internal collector over the peering/privatelink) or we can disable certain telemetry during the poc. any external dependencies (like external APIs) would need explicit exceptions.
[04:39] Maya Patel: sounds fine. about regions — we need the inference to run in eu-west-2 (London) for UK data residency concerns, and for EU mainland we prefer eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 depending on latency. can you host in London?
[04:52] Daniel Ortiz: yes we have capacity options in eu-west-2; for the poc we can allocate nodes in eu-west-2 and optionally mirror in eu-west-1 for comparison. Note: certain GPU instance SKUs can be limited in eu-west-2; we'll confirm availability in the next 48 hours.
[05:06] Laura Kim: and if eu-west-2 capacity is constrained we can offer eu-west-1 with PrivateLink and a routing policy to keep data in-region — but you are right, best to check availability now.
[05:15] Rajiv Menon: benchmark design question: can Redwood run the benchmarks from your side against our endpoint, or do we need to generate traffic from our infra to validate actual networking e2e latency?
[05:25] Daniel Ortiz: we recommend doing both. Redwood can run a server-side benchmark to confirm model runtime performance in our infra, but for true e2e latency (including your network, firewall, and any HSM/KMS calls) it's better if you run the load generators inside your VPC targeting the PrivateLink/peering path. we can provide the test harness and scripts.
[05:43] Maya Patel: ok we'll run them from our infra. timeline for tests — we need to plan a dry-run, then a production-like run. can you propose dates?
[05:51] Laura Kim: propose dry-run Nov 30, then full benchmark Dec 1-3 (we'll block windows and coordinate capacity). that gives a week to exchange artifacts and configure endpoints. does that work?
[06:01] Sofia Alvarez: tight but workable. i'll need the security pack and the network diagrams asap.
[06:06] Laura Kim: noted. on authentication — we support SAML/SSO for console access and API keys for service auth. For the poc we typically provision a least-privilege API key scoped to the environment and rotate it after. Is that acceptable?
[06:18] Maya Patel: yes, as long as we can rotate and audit usage. also need RBAC for who can call what.
[06:23] Daniel Ortiz: RBAC is supported; we can create roles for dev, infra, and security. Audit logs tie back to user identity if users use SSO.
[06:31] Rajiv Menon: a few practical constraints: our outbound firewall only allows specific destination ports and hostnames. with PrivateLink we just need to open to the VPC endpoint; with peering we'd need to add route table entries and security group rules. which one will minimize coordination with our ops team?
[06:46] Daniel Ortiz: PrivateLink generally minimizes route table changes and is easier with strict egress, since traffic to the endpoint stays inside AWS and you control the endpoint's security groups. Peering can be simple too if both sides agree on routes, but it touches route tables. Given your firewall constraints, PrivateLink looks lower friction.
[07:02] Maya Patel: ok leaning PrivateLink then. can you put together a step-by-step PrivateLink runbook we can hand to ops?
[07:08] Laura Kim: yes, we'll include a ops runbook with exact ENI steps, required SG rules, sample route checks, and CIDR examples. we'll also include our recommended instance types and expected throughput.
[07:18] Daniel Ortiz: quick note on costs: PrivateLink has data processing fees per GB plus our dedicated capacity cost; peering avoids endpoint charges but may require Transit GW costs for cross-account patterns. we'll put a preliminary cost estimate in the poc doc.
[07:34] Sofia Alvarez: for data residency again — even if the runtime is in London, some logs or meta could still be accessible from other accounts for ops. can you guarantee logs and traces for the poc remain in our S3 bucket in eu-west-2 only?
[07:47] Daniel Ortiz: for Hosted PrivateLink we can configure cross-account S3 writes directly to your bucket in eu-west-2 using your KMS key; logs won't be replicated outside unless you request. We'll document retention and access controls. For Private on-prem we have full control with local storage.
[08:01] Maya Patel: great. can we talk about success criteria in more detail and a pass/fail rubric?
[08:06] Laura Kim: yes, suggested pass/fail:
- Networking: no external public egress authenticated during the poc (pass if all traffic flows through PrivateLink/peering and validated by packet captures)
- Residency: all customer data and logs written to eu-west-2 S3 using customer's KMS (pass if audit shows writes only to that bucket)
- Performance: p95 latency < 150ms over a sustained 30 minute window at 50 RPS using your production prompt set (pass if p95 < 150ms; marginal if 150–200ms)
- Stability: no unexplained errors > 5% over the run window
- Observability: traces and token-level cost breakdown available post-run

[08:48] Rajiv Menon: that looks clear. one more on benchmarks: we sometimes see tokenization differences across runtime/SDKs — do you support the same tokenizer and token counting we use?
[08:57] Daniel Ortiz: yes, we can use the same tokenizer version you use (we've supported tiktoken and other tokenizers). we'll include tokenization in the harness to ensure parity.
[09:06] Maya Patel: ok next — timeline and approvals. Our procurement needs SOW and pricing; security needs the pack; infra needs the runbook. if we agree to the proposed dates and artifacts i think we can get approvals in two weeks.
[09:19] Laura Kim: we'll produce a short SOW for the 4-week poc and include deliverables: runbook, benchmark harness, security pack, dedicated capacity, and a final report. we'll include cost bands for the dedicated nodes and PrivateLink egress.
[09:33] Sofia Alvarez: please make the SOW explicit about who retains logs and how long traces persist. we need a 90-day retention limit for this poc at most.
[09:42] Laura Kim: noted, we'll set retention to 90 days for traces in the poc config.
[09:47] Maya Patel: any blockers we're missing?
[09:50] Daniel Ortiz: one near-term item is confirming GPU SKU availability in eu-west-2. i'll check quota and availability and report back in 48 hours.
[09:59] Laura Kim: and i'll share the security pack + initial cost sheet by end of day tomorrow.
[10:05] Rajiv Menon: i'll share the VPC CIDRs and the egress firewall doc by tomorrow.
[10:10] Sofia Alvarez: good. also please include contact for our SOC person — i'll cc them once the pack is shared.
[10:15] Laura Kim: will do.
[10:17] Maya Patel: cool thanks everyone, let's reconvene after the docs are shared and schedule the dry run.
[10:22] Laura Kim: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the Nov 30 dry-run and Dec 1-3 windows, and upload the runbook to the shared link.
[10:28] (end)
